source.title: Frankenstein Optimizer: Harnessing the Potential by Revisiting Optimization Tricks
source.authors: Chia-Wei Hsu; Nien-Ti Tsou; Yu-Cheng Chen; Y. Park; Ju Li

record.file_problem: The supplied full text includes some malformed or flattened table content, but the relevant prose and appendix results are present.
record.tranche_reason: Compares adaptive optimizers, SGD, and a new optimizer on held-out performance, using different tasks and measures from the cited optimizer studies.
record.gate_note: Results cited from prior studies are not extracted. The paper reports its own optimizer comparisons, including held-out accuracy or loss and qualitative test-set findings. Some results are described only in figures; no precise values are inferred from them.
record.test_reason: The study uses adaptive optimizers' reported generalization disadvantage to motivate Frankenstein and evaluates its own method. The supplied results do not establish an adaptive-versus-SGD held-out comparison under V4's tuning conditions. Sophia versus Frankenstein compares two adaptive methods; Adam's spikes and representation drift do not establish worse generalization than SGD.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that Frankenstein improves convergence and generalization across their tested applications and offers benefits in scientific optimization. Their claims of broad superiority concern their proposed optimizer and do not independently establish V4's adaptive-versus-SGD comparison.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces Frankenstein, a new optimizer, and compares it with existing optimizers across several tasks; experiments use task-specific tuning in several settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports results across different tasks, architectures, epoch counts, sequence lengths, and sequence-length grouping. In the Alpaca fine-tuning experiment, Adam's test-set behavior is affected by grouping sequences by length.

fits_no_version.finding: Frankenstein achieves the reported best accuracy on four EfficientNet variants and superior qualitative generalization on the IMDB task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed Frankenstein optimizer improves held-out performance relative to its tested competitors in some settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Sophia reaches lower training loss but worse test loss than Frankenstein during LLaMA-7B instruction fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different adaptive optimizers can exhibit different degrees of overfitting during instruction fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam exhibits test-loss spikes with length-grouped sequences, and Adam/RMSProp models exhibit greater representational divergence during image fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects training stability and representational drift; these measures alone do not establish the adaptive-versus-SGD generalization ordering.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix D reports CIFAR-10 test accuracy of 93.17 ± 0.17 for Frankenstein and 92.12 ± 0.17 for Adam; Appendix E reports robust test convergence for Frankenstein on a synthetic binary task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frankenstein can outperform another adaptive optimizer on held-out performance, including in a synthetic overfitting demonstration.

record.problems: Several task comparisons are qualitative or figure-based without numerical values in the text. The ImageNet table is flattened in the supplied text, preventing reliable assignment of most optimizer values. The experiments do not directly quantify train-test gaps for most tasks.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for the neural-network quantum-state optimization figure: it reports optimization loss, not held-out natural-label performance. No rows for materials simulations, which do not measure the claim's model generalization behavior.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization using the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.

A recoverable comparison of existing adaptive optimizers against SGD under limited tuning; changes to that comparison under broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, optimizer switching, or word-level language modeling. Appendix B reports tuning, including potentially individual weight-decay tuning, but does not isolate its effect on the adaptive–SGD difference.

Large versus small batches on image or language workloads under fixed epoch budgets, including adaptations that remove the penalty. Appendix E's synthetic binary task does not establish this comparison.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on training-set size, dropout strength, or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps among networks with similarly low training loss, including comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are warranted from the supplied rows. Figure captions identify optimizer comparisons but do not supply readable curves or adaptive-versus-SGD outcomes. Appendix E's batch-size comparison and Section 4's landscape visualization do not establish V5 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of fitting random labels against generalization on natural labels.
No width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

The paper compares optimizers on its own tasks, but does not test the claim's limited-tuning condition or broad tuning, decoupled weight decay, or switching from Adam to SGD. It does not report the word-level language-model comparison described in the version.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer test error on ImageNet-1K; Frankenstein results are reported at 40, 80, and 120 epochs.
rows.note: The text says Frankenstein is comparable to Adam in 40 epochs and to Adan and AdaFisher in 80 epochs for ResNet18. No complete comparator values are recoverable from the supplied flattened table.
rows.check: These are Frankenstein's own validation errors, without a recoverable adaptive-versus-SGD comparison. Table 2 also incorporates cited comparator results with different training budgets; those are not this study's own controlled comparisons.

rows.subject: EfficientNetB0-6
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer test accuracy across EfficientNet architectures.
rows.value: Frankenstein got the best accuracy for B1, B2, B5, and B6
rows.note: The statement identifies four architectures but gives no corresponding accuracy values; it does not establish a result for B0, B3, or B4.
rows.check: Frankenstein winning on four architectures evaluates the proposed method, without reporting Adam or another existing adaptive optimizer's performance relative to SGD. It does not establish partial occurrence of V4.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1.2, lines 525–533, continuing at lines 423–426; Figure 2 caption.

rows.subject: BERT with two GRU layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizers on binary sentiment classification and reported test accuracy profiles.
rows.value: Frankenstein achieved superior generalization, as shown in Fig. 3
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison, without specific values or naming the competing optimizers in this result statement.
rows.check: The qualitative result concerns Frankenstein's superiority and supplies no adaptive-versus-SGD ordering. The fixed learning-rate condition is also uncertain: Section 3.2.1 specifies 2 × 10−4, whereas Appendix B reports a learning-rate search and tenfold larger rates for SGD.

source_check.problem: The condition matches Section 3.2.1, but Appendix B conflicts with its fixed learning-rate account by reporting optimizer-specific tuning.

rows.subject: LLaMA-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimizer training and test loss in instruction fine-tuning.
rows.baseline: Frankenstein test loss not numerically stated
rows.value: Sophia achieved lower training loss than Frankenstein but worse test loss
rows.note: This is a qualitative result; the text does not give loss values.
rows.check: The Sophia–Frankenstein training/test loss ordering is accurately extracted, but both are adaptive optimizers. Overfitting relative to Frankenstein does not establish V4's disadvantage relative to SGD.

rows.subject: LLaMA-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Adam's test-loss behavior during instruction fine-tuning.
rows.value: Adam showed performance spikes on the test set
rows.note: The authors attribute the spikes to grouping sequences by length and describe them as reflecting training instability; the text gives no numerical comparison.
rows.check: Test-loss spikes indicate instability in the reported setting, without establishing worse held-out performance than SGD. They cannot be classified as partial occurrence of V4.

rows.subject: EfficientNetB0
rows.operation_detail: Compared final representations of Adam- or RMSProp-trained models with their initial pretrained representations using CKA.
rows.value: Models trained with Adam or RMSProp showed greater divergence in their final representations
rows.note: This representation result is discussed in connection with overfitting but does not directly measure the train-test generalization gap named by V4; omitted from V4 verdict labels.
rows.check: CKA divergence measures representational change, not held-out performance relative to SGD. It also does not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its association with generalization gaps.

relation.reason: The reported disadvantage motivates optimizer design, while the extracted results evaluate Frankenstein or compare adaptive methods with each other. Appendix E's synthetic overfitting experiment supplies no explicit adaptive-versus-SGD result on V4's image or language benchmarks.

tranche.reason: The study motivates and evaluates Frankenstein using reported adaptive-optimizer generalization problems. The supplied text does not establish an existing adaptive-versus-SGD ordering under V4's tuning conditions; its CKA analysis also does not test V7.

source_check.notes: Section 3.2.1 specifies a shared learning rate of 2 × 10−4; Appendix B instead reports an NLU learning-rate search and possible individual weight-decay tuning. The authors' broad superiority conclusion is accurately summarized, but does not establish V4.
